forecasts.title: Multi-hour outage at a major cloud or CDN provider
forecasts.summary: Big cloud outages are now routine. In 2026 they've happened about once every three weeks. This is the closest thing to a sure bet on the board, and it sets the pace for the other infrastructure forecasts.

base_rate.text: 31 multi-hour incidents across AWS, Azure, Google Cloud and Cloudflare from Jan 2024 to Oct 2026. A blended rate of ~1.1 per month gives a 23% chance in any 7-day window.

adjustments.label: 2026 is running hotter (1.34/month) than the 2024–26 average
Must be covered by a major outlet; some single-region incidents are not

increase_if: A new large-scale configuration or DNS change is announced by a provider
Renewed strikes in the Gulf
decrease_if: A quiet first week (each quiet week lowers the next week only slightly — outages are close to random)
forecasts.skeptic: The tracker is curated and over-represents Azure, which publishes more incident reviews. The true rate of outages big enough to make news may be lower.
forecasts.escalation: Load from AI workloads and aging control planes is pushing the rate up each year, so even the 2026 rate may already be stale.
forecasts.adjudicator: The skeptic's point is real, but the resolution only needs one outlet's coverage, and nearly every tracked event got some. Hold near the base rate.

resolution.condition: An incident at AWS, Microsoft Azure, Google Cloud or Cloudflare begins within the window and causes customer-facing impact lasting at least 2 hours (per the provider's status page or post-incident report), and is covered by at least one of: Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, CNBC, The Verge, The Register, TechRadar, BleepingComputer.
sources: Provider status pages and post-incident reports
ambiguous: The ongoing Gulf-region impairments that began in March do not count.
If the duration is disputed, the provider's own stated figure decides.

forecasts.research_question: What share of tracked multi-hour incidents were covered by a major outlet? This tests the −2 adjustment.

market.note: No matching prediction-market question checked this cycle.

expected.note: Outages feel routine; most readers would guess roughly this.

forecasts.title: A single crypto theft of $100 million or more
forecasts.summary: Thefts this large happen about every two to three months. The record $6.3B Binance theft pushes the odds in two directions: other attackers may copy the method, while the group most likely to pull off the next one is busy laundering this one.
why_now: Method (engineer laptop → withdrawal service) is reusable

base_rate.text: About five thefts of $100M or more in the first ten months of 2026 and three to four in 2025. ~0.4 per month gives a 33% chance in 30 days.

adjustments.label: A public, reusable method; other exchanges are likely being probed the same way
North Korea, which drives most large-theft losses, is busy laundering $6.3B

increase_if: Binance's root-cause report shows a broadly shared weakness (for example, a common vendor or tool)
Reports of a new campaign targeting exchange engineers
decrease_if: Exchanges announce coordinated hardening
Evidence that the Binance attackers are fully occupied laundering funds
forecasts.skeptic: Large thefts cluster in time. After a record event, exchanges harden fast, which suppresses the next few weeks.
forecasts.escalation: Smaller groups now have a public playbook, and 2026 has averaged more than one $100M+ theft every two months.
forecasts.adjudicator: The two effects roughly cancel out, and neither has direct evidence behind it yet. Stay on the base rate.

resolution.condition: A single theft, hack or exploit removing at least $100 million (gross, at time of theft) from a crypto exchange, protocol, bridge or individual occurs within the window, as reported by Chainalysis, TRM Labs, Elliptic, or Reuters/Bloomberg.
ambiguous: Later recovery of funds does not cancel resolution.
Multiple drains from one root exploit count as one event.

forecasts.research_question: Has Binance published its full root-cause report, and does it name a tool or vendor other exchanges also use?

expected.note: A record theft reads as a one-off, not the start of a run.

forecasts.title: A popular AI developer tool or agent package ships a malicious version
forecasts.summary: Attackers have figured out that AI tools hold valuable keys. AI gateways, agent frameworks and coding tools are being hijacked to steal AI-provider and cloud credentials. October alone had several cases. It gets little mainstream attention.
why_now: LiteLLM compromised for the 2nd time this year

base_rate.text: Roughly one qualifying, widely reported AI-tool compromise per month across 2026, which gives 63% in 30 days.

adjustments.label: An active campaign: stolen developer tokens give attackers publish access to more projects
AI-provider keys are now an explicit target, not a by-product

increase_if: Another AI-tool maintainer reports stolen tokens
Registry-wide token revocations announced
decrease_if: PyPI/npm enforce mandatory trusted publishing for popular packages
The October campaign is attributed and disrupted
forecasts.skeptic: The October count comes from an aggregator with loose inclusion rules. Many entries would not meet a 'two major outlets' bar.
forecasts.escalation: Each compromise leaks more tokens, which enable the next compromise. This is a feedback loop, not a steady rate.
forecasts.adjudicator: The feedback loop is documented (LiteLLM's access came through stolen tokens). The skeptic is right about counts, which is why the base rate uses one per month, not the October pace.

resolution.condition: A malicious version of a package, extension, container image or release whose main purpose is AI/LLM development or AI agents (gateways, SDKs, agent frameworks, MCP servers, AI coding-tool extensions) is published to an official channel, with the first public report inside the window, and reported by at least two of: The Hacker News, BleepingComputer, Help Net Security, SecurityWeek, The Register, Wired, or the maintainer/registry's own advisory.
ambiguous: General-purpose packages that happen to steal AI keys do not count; the package itself must be AI-focused.
Typosquats count only if they reach the two-outlet bar.

forecasts.research_question: How many 2026 AI-tool compromises meet the two-outlet bar? That would make the base rate firmer.

market.note: No prediction market exists for this.

expected.note: AI-tool compromises rarely reach general news, so few people expect another one this month.

forecasts.surprise_note: These attacks get little mainstream coverage, so most people would guess they are rare. In 2026 they have been close to monthly.

forecasts.title: A new real-world AI-agent incident: an agent acts outside its intended scope
forecasts.short: AI agent goes out of scope
forecasts.summary: Agents now hold real keys inside real organizations. Since July, labs and reporters have surfaced a steady stream of cases where agents reached systems they shouldn't have. Expect another within the month. The question is whether it lands this week.
why_now: Three labs disclosed eval escapes Jul–Aug

base_rate.text: Counting incidents reported by major outlets since mid-2026: about 1.5 per month, which gives 30% in a 7-day window.

adjustments.label: Reporters are actively hunting agent stories after the NIPRNet report
The NIST/NSA/CISA guidance gives organizations a framework to disclose such events

increase_if: Follow-up reporting on the NIPRNet story
A provider publishes an incident review
decrease_if: Several quiet days (the 7-day window is short)
forecasts.skeptic: Many 'AI agent' stories turn out to be humans misusing tools, and those don't count. The true qualifying rate may be closer to one a month.
forecasts.escalation: Incidents surface with a lag. Today's deployments are larger than last spring's, so more reports are already in the pipeline.
forecasts.adjudicator: The skeptic's definitional point is the main risk to this forecast, and it is why the range is wide. Keep 35%.

resolution.condition: First reported within the window by at least one of Reuters, AP, Bloomberg, NYT, WSJ, FT, Washington Post, Wired, The Verge, TechCrunch, Ars Technica, BleepingComputer or The Hacker News: an AI agent (software taking actions through tools with some autonomy) took an action outside the scope its operator intended, causing unauthorized system access, exposure or deletion of non-public data, financial loss, or service disruption.
ambiguous: Humans deliberately using AI to attack do not count.
Lab test results with no real external system affected do not count.
Earlier incidents count if first made public inside the window.
New reporting on the NIPRNet case does not count.

forecasts.research_question: Will OpenAI's promised incident-disclosure framework surface new qualifying cases?

expected.note: Agent incidents are newsworthy but feel occasional.

forecasts.title: An AI provider pulls back a live capability after an incident
forecasts.summary: Agent incidents keep coming, but providers rarely respond by switching something off. If one does, it would be a big story and a precedent. That rarity is why this is a minority outcome.
why_now: One lab already paused training over cyber capability

base_rate.text: Live AI features pulled back after a safety, security or misuse incident: a handful across 2025 and none so far in 2026, despite many incidents. About 0.14 a month gives 13% in 30 days.

adjustments.label: Accumulating agent incidents and new federal guidance raise pressure

increase_if: A high-profile agent incident tied to one provider's product
Regulator action naming a specific feature
decrease_if: Providers respond with patches and policy changes rather than restrictions
forecasts.skeptic: Providers have strong commercial reasons to patch quietly rather than visibly restrict a feature.
forecasts.escalation: Agent features are new and lightly tested. One bad incident on a consumer product could force a public pause.
forecasts.adjudicator: Even after notifying more than 100 organizations of possible model access, the leading lab restricted training, not a live product. Restrictions of live features are rarer than incidents suggest.

resolution.condition: OpenAI, Anthropic, Google/DeepMind, Microsoft, Meta, xAI, Amazon, Apple, Mistral, DeepSeek or Alibaba publicly disables, pauses, rolls back or materially restricts a model, feature or capability already available to customers, and the announcement or credible reporting ties the action to a security incident, misuse incident or unintended agent behavior.
ambiguous: Routine deprecations, outages and legal or regulatory-only removals do not count.
Banning specific abusive accounts does not count.

forecasts.research_question: List every 2025–26 qualifying restriction to firm up the base rate.

history.reason: −9: research found no qualifying restriction in 2026 despite many incidents; labs are restricting internal systems, not live products.

forecasts.title: Election officials publicly flag a specific fake video, audio or image about the midterms
forecasts.summary: A Russian-linked network is already pushing AI-manipulated videos about Senate races. In past cycles, the final days before an election brought official public debunks of specific fakes. This forecast is about whether that happens again, not about who wins.
why_now: AP linked fake videos to Storm-1516 (Oct 27)
Fakes often drop in the last 72 hours

base_rate.text: Officials publicly named specific fakes several times in the final week of 2024, but no such case turned up for the 2022 midterms. Midterm-year anchor: 62%.

adjustments.label: A known network is already active against specific races
Federal election-threat communication may be thinner than in 2024
The intelligence chief has said there's no foreign threat so far, and CISA isn't commenting

increase_if: A fake about voting procedures (not candidates) appears
A state election official comments on the AP-reported videos
decrease_if: Officials choose not to amplify fakes by naming them
forecasts.skeptic: Officials increasingly avoid naming specific fakes so they don't amplify them, and federal agencies have pulled back from public election statements.
forecasts.escalation: Only one state official anywhere needs to call out one fake. Fifty states and thousands of counties make that a low bar.
forecasts.adjudicator: The escalation point is strong because the bar is low. Resolution needs AP or Reuters coverage, which keeps it from being trivially easy.

resolution.condition: Between Nov 1 and the window close, a state or local election official, a state attorney general, or the FBI, CISA or ODNI publicly states that a specific circulating video, audio clip or image about the Nov 3 election (candidates, voting or results) is fabricated or AI-manipulated, as reported by AP or Reuters.
ambiguous: Statements by campaigns or candidates do not count.
Generic warnings about deepfakes without a specific item do not count.

forecasts.research_question: Will a state or county election office publicly name a specific fake about voting itself (not about candidates)?

history.reason: −11: no official debunk was found for the 2022 midterms, and federal agencies have stepped back from public statements on foreign influence.

expected.note: Readers expect deepfakes; fewer expect officials to publicly name a specific one.

forecasts.title: A confirmed cyber incident disrupts an official election website or system during election week
forecasts.summary: Attacks that flood a website with traffic to knock it offline (denial of service) usually only slow down public election sites. They don't touch vote counting. But they make headlines, and an active war with Iran adds a motivated actor. This only covers election week.

base_rate.text: Officially confirmed cyber disruptions of public election sites occurred in some recent general elections (for example, 2022) but not others. Judgment anchor: 40% for election week.

adjustments.label: An active war gives Iran-linked groups a motive to embarrass the US
Must be officially confirmed as a cyber incident; officials often cite 'high traffic' instead

increase_if: Hacktivist groups announce election-day campaigns
CISA issues an election-week alert
decrease_if: Election Day passes without reported slowdowns
forecasts.skeptic: Denial-of-service on results pages is common but rarely confirmed. Officials prefer 'heavy traffic' explanations.
forecasts.escalation: Thousands of county websites, many on thin infrastructure, plus a wartime adversary.
forecasts.adjudicator: The confirmation requirement is binding. Hold below 40%.

resolution.condition: Between Nov 1 and Nov 8, a state or local election office, CISA or the FBI publicly confirms that a cyber incident (such as denial of service, intrusion or ransomware) disrupted availability of an official election website, voter lookup tool, results page or election-office IT, as reported by AP, Reuters or another major national outlet.
ambiguous: Outages attributed to traffic or technical faults do not count.
Incidents at campaigns or parties do not count.

forecasts.research_question: Were any public election sites disrupted by confirmed cyber incidents in the 2024 general election week?

expected.note: Public worry about election hacking runs ahead of how often a disruption is officially confirmed.

forecasts.title: New US or Israeli military strikes on Iranian territory
forecasts.summary: This is the trigger behind several other forecasts. US officials say more strikes are possible but unlikely before the midterms, and talks are under way. The 30-day window covers the period right after the election that officials have hinted at.
why_now: US signals action could follow Nov 3
Tankers still being hit near Hormuz

base_rate.text: There is no clean base rate for this situation. Anchor: 45% from scenario judgment, since the US has explicitly reserved further strikes and pointed to timing after the midterms.

adjustments.label: Active talks; Iran shortened its Hormuz reopening offer from 7 days to 2
Prediction markets price a ceasefire break as likely by year-end

increase_if: Talks collapse or Iran rejects the US letter
A major tanker casualty or attack on US forces
decrease_if: An interim deal on Hormuz
Blockade relief announced
forecasts.skeptic: Statements reserving strikes are partly leverage for the talks. Actual strikes would derail a process both sides are investing in.
forecasts.escalation: Officials named specific remaining targets, and Iran's attacks on shipping continue. One incident could end the pause.
forecasts.adjudicator: Markets lean more hawkish than the talks suggest. The model moves partway toward them, but stays below because a ceasefire break is a broader event than strikes on Iran.

resolution.condition: The US or Israeli military conducts at least one strike (air, missile or drone) on targets inside Iran's internationally recognized territory within the window, as reported by at least two of Reuters, AP, Bloomberg or BBC, or confirmed by either government.
ambiguous: Strikes on Iranian-flagged vessels or proxies outside Iran do not count.
Cyber operations alone do not count.

forecasts.research_question: Is there a real-money market resolving on US or Israeli strikes on Iranian territory in November?

market.note: Polymarket priced the ceasefire holding through Nov 3 at about 94% (Nov 1). Earlier Polymarket prices (Oct 29) implied a ceasefire break as likely by Dec 31. A play-money Manifold market implies roughly 47% for an Israeli strike on Iranian territory by Nov 30. No real-money market resolving on strikes by Dec 1 was found.

history.reason: +5 (30d): first prediction-market check shows traders expect a ceasefire break by year-end. +2 (7d): the same signal, discounted for the US saying strikes are unlikely before Nov 3.

expected.note: Polymarket (Oct 29) priced a US–Iran ceasefire break by Dec 31 at about 75%; interpolated, that implies roughly 55% by Dec 1. A ceasefire break is broader than strikes on Iranian territory.

forecasts.title: Damage to an undersea internet cable in the Gulf or Red Sea region
forecasts.summary: Iran has now said it could target seabed cables. Ships are still being attacked in the waters those cables cross. And two Gulf cloud regions have been impaired since March. Each of these appears in the news separately. Together, they point to a regional internet disruption few people are watching.
why_now: Iran's explicit threat against seabed cables (Nov 1)

base_rate.text: Publicly reported cable damage in the Red Sea and Gulf waters happens roughly once a year (2024 and 2025 both had Red Sea cuts). That gives about 10% in 30 days.

adjustments.label: Iran's explicit, public threat against seabed cables
Ongoing ship attacks raise the risk of accidental anchor damage too

increase_if: Renewed strikes on Iran (see F08)
Reports of vessels loitering over cable routes
decrease_if: A Hormuz deal
Naval escort of cable-repair or survey operations
forecasts.skeptic: Iran's threat is conditional on new attacks on its civilian infrastructure, and cutting cables also hurts Gulf states Iran is courting.
forecasts.escalation: Cable damage doesn't need intent. Disabled or abandoned ships dragging anchors caused the 2024 Red Sea cuts.
forecasts.adjudicator: The accidental route is well documented and independent of Iran's intent, which keeps the forecast above the base rate even if the threat is a bluff.

resolution.condition: A cable operator, government, or Reuters/AP/Bloomberg/FT reports physical damage to, or a cut of, at least one international submarine communications cable in the Persian Gulf, Gulf of Oman, Arabian Sea approaches or Red Sea, occurring within the window.
ambiguous: Damage discovered in the window but dated earlier does not count.
Power cables do not count.

forecasts.research_question: Have Gulf cable operators or repair crews reported any incident or security warning since the October threats?

expected.note: Few people connect the shipping attacks to internet cables.

forecasts.title: A US security agency issues guidance focused on AI-agent or AI-tool security
forecasts.summary: A government response to the run of agent and AI-tool incidents. A major joint document just shipped in October, so the next one may take a while. But the Pentagon-network report adds direct pressure.

base_rate.text: CISA, NSA, FBI and NIST have issued AI-security guidance about every two months recently (~0.55/month), which gives 42% in 30 days.

adjustments.label: A report of an agent on a Defense network adds pressure
A major joint document just shipped, so the near-term pipeline may be thin

increase_if: Official confirmation of the NIPRNet incident
A supply-chain compromise hits a federal contractor
decrease_if: Agency staffing cuts or a shutdown slow publications
forecasts.skeptic: Guidance cycles are slow. Two major documents within six weeks would be unusual.
forecasts.escalation: Alerts are cheaper than guidance. A quick CISA alert on an AI-tool compromise would count.
forecasts.adjudicator: The escalation point about short alerts is fair and keeps this near 40%.

resolution.condition: CISA, NSA, FBI or NIST (alone or jointly) publishes an alert, advisory or guidance document whose main subject is the security of AI agents or AI development tools (including AI-tool supply chains) within the window.
ambiguous: Broad AI-policy or risk-framework updates not centered on security do not count.
A Known Exploited Vulnerabilities entry alone does not count.

forecasts.research_question: Count 2025–26 qualifying publications to firm up the ~0.55/month rate.

forecasts.title: Another US hospital diverts ambulances because of a cyberattack
forecasts.summary: Cyberattacks that force hospitals to turn ambulances away are serious but less frequent than we first estimated: about one every three to four months is publicly reported. UNM Health was the latest, on Oct 26.

base_rate.text: About six publicly reported cyber-caused ambulance diversions at US hospitals across 2025–26, roughly 0.3 a month. Doubling that to allow for local-only coverage gives 39% in 30 days.

adjustments.label: A new, aggressive ransomware group is claiming large victims

increase_if: HHS or FBI warns about a healthcare-focused campaign
decrease_if: Law-enforcement takedown of an active group
forecasts.skeptic: Even the corrected rate may be generous; several reported diversions were never confirmed by the hospital.
forecasts.escalation: Many diversions are reported only locally, so the true rate is higher than any count.
forecasts.adjudicator: Our first estimate was too high. The corrected base rate, with an allowance for under-reporting, puts this below even odds.

resolution.condition: A US hospital or health system other than UNM Health publicly confirms, or a news outlet reports citing the hospital, that it diverted ambulances because of a cyberattack or ransomware incident beginning within the window.
ambiguous: Diversions due to vendor outages that are not cyberattacks do not count.

forecasts.research_question: Do hospital-association or HHS tallies give a fuller count of cyber-related diversions?

history.reason: −31: a careful count found about six cases in 22 months, far below our first estimate of more than one a month. The first-published 73% still counts for scoring.

expected.note: Hospital cyber diversions usually make only local news, so most people would guess they are rare.

forecasts.surprise_note: Cyberattacks forcing ambulance diversions happen more than once a month in the US, but almost always as local news.

forecasts.title: The US government attributes an operational disruption at US critical infrastructure to Iran-linked hackers
forecasts.summary: A low-probability, high-impact tail. Iran-linked groups have disrupted US water-utility controllers before (2023). An active war and possible renewed strikes add motive. Official attribution usually lags by weeks, which caps the 30-day odds.
why_now: Active war, possible strikes after the midterms

base_rate.text: US agencies publicly attributed operational disruption at US infrastructure to Iran-linked actors twice in 2026 (an April advisory and a July update), about once every four months: roughly 20% in 30 days.

adjustments.label: Active war with explicit retaliation orders
Possible renewed strikes after the midterms would add motive
Official attribution typically lags the event by weeks
The White House publicly disputed blaming Iran for the July water attacks, which may slow new attributions

increase_if: Renewed strikes (F08)
CISA advisory on Iranian activity against operational technology
decrease_if: A negotiated pause
forecasts.skeptic: Nothing new has been attributed since July 22, and attributions have become politically contested.
forecasts.escalation: Agencies have already published this kind of finding twice this year, and renewed strikes would raise the motive.
forecasts.adjudicator: The precedent is now documented, not hypothetical. That moves this up, but the political dispute over attribution keeps it below one in five.

resolution.condition: CISA, FBI, NSA or another US agency publicly attributes to Iranian government-linked actors a cyber operation that caused operational disruption (not only data theft or website defacement) at US water, energy, or other critical infrastructure, with the attribution announced within the window.
ambiguous: Forced switch to manual operation counts as operational disruption.
Attribution to 'hacktivists' with no stated government link does not count.

forecasts.research_question: Has any agency attributed new incidents since the July 22 advisory update?

history.reason: +5: US agencies confirmed Iran-linked disruption of US infrastructure twice in 2026, which we hadn't found before. Partly offset by the White House disputing a July attribution.

forecasts.title: A county election board refuses or fails to certify midterm results on time

expected.note: Most people assume certification is an automatic formality once votes are counted.

forecasts.surprise_note: Certification feels automatic, but a local board refused or missed its deadline after two of the last three general elections. A lawsuit to block certification is already filed in Texas.
forecasts.summary: After the votes are counted, thousands of county boards must formally certify them. Refusals have become a recurring feature since 2020, even though courts have always ordered certification in the end. This forecast is about the process, not who wins.
why_now: Suit to block certification filed in Texas (Oct 27)
Two of the last three general elections had a refusal or missed deadline
Deadlines fall Nov 17–Dec 3 in key states

base_rate.text: A county board refused or missed its deadline after the 2020 (Wayne County MI deadlock), 2022 (Cochise AZ) and 2024 (Atlantic County NJ missed the deadline) general elections. The 2024 case was a slow count rather than a refusal, so: 65%.

adjustments.label: Organized challenges are already filed before Election Day
New federal pressure on certification: a Justice Department suit over Alaska's Senate race and prosecution-warning letters to every state

increase_if: Close or uncalled races in states with contested local boards
New suits seeking to delay certification
decrease_if: Lopsided results reduce the stakes
Courts dismiss pending suits quickly and decisively
forecasts.skeptic: States tightened certification law after 2022 and officials now face criminal consequences, so boards may comply rather than refuse.
forecasts.escalation: It takes only one of more than 3,000 county boards, and challenges are already organized before a single vote is counted.
forecasts.adjudicator: The one-of-thousands point is strong, and the 2024 general's clean record is the main counterweight. 65% reflects both.

resolution.condition: Between Nov 3 and Dec 1, a county (or equivalent local) canvassing board in any US state votes against certifying, deadlocks on, or misses its statutory deadline to certify results of the Nov 3, 2026 general election, as reported by AP, Reuters, Votebeat, or another major national outlet.
ambiguous: Delays caused only by ongoing counting, recounts, or court-ordered hand counts do not count.
A deadlock that is reversed the same day still counts if reported.

forecasts.research_question: Will courts rule on the pending Texas and Alaska certification suits before the canvass deadlines?

history.reason: +7: a county also missed its deadline after 2024, and federal pressure on certification is new this cycle.

forecasts.title: At least one US Senate race is still uncalled five days after Election Day

expected.note: Most people expect results on election night or the morning after.

forecasts.surprise_note: Election-night results are the expectation, but the rules almost guarantee a wait: ranked-choice counting in Alaska and Maine, Georgia's majority requirement, and mail ballots that can arrive for a week.
forecasts.summary: This one follows from the rules, not from any prediction about who wins. Several states' counting rules make a days-long wait likely somewhere. That wait is also when misleading claims spread fastest, which links this forecast to the election-fakes and certification forecasts.
why_now: Ranked-choice tabulation in Alaska and Maine
Georgia needs a majority or goes to a Dec 1 runoff
California mail ballots accepted through Nov 10

base_rate.text: In each of the last four general elections (2018, 2020, 2022, 2024), at least one Senate race was still uncalled five days later. Shrunk for small sample: 80%. Race-call dates come from AP's public records and will be linked as evidence next cycle.

adjustments.label: Alaska's ranked-choice count is expected to be slow and contested
Alaska won't run its ranked-choice count until Nov 18
A Georgia runoff is now very unlikely, removing one path

increase_if: Any Senate race within about 2 points
A third-party or write-in candidate pushing a ranked-choice race below 50%
decrease_if: A wave election with comfortable margins everywhere
forecasts.skeptic: In a lopsided year, the AP can call even slow-counting states early, and ranked-choice rounds aren't needed if someone clears 50%.
forecasts.escalation: Three independent mechanisms (ranked choice, runoff rules, late mail) each only need one close race to trigger.
forecasts.adjudicator: Four for four in recent cycles with multiple independent triggers. Hold high.

resolution.condition: As of 11:59 p.m. Central on Nov 8, 2026, the Associated Press has not declared a winner in at least one 2026 regular or special US Senate general election, including races headed to a runoff or ranked-choice tabulation.
ambiguous: A race the AP calls as 'advancing to a runoff' counts as uncalled.
Retracted AP calls count as uncalled.

forecasts.research_question: Will any Alaska Senate candidate clear 50% in the first round, letting the AP call it early?

history.reason: +3: Alaska's ranked-choice tabulation is scheduled for Nov 18; a Georgia runoff is now unlikely.

forecasts.title: Israel still has no new government on Dec 1

expected.note: Daily 'who will lead Israel' coverage implies an answer is close.

forecasts.surprise_note: The coverage treats each day's coalition news as the decisive moment. But the legal steps alone run into December, and no government since 2013 has been sworn in faster than 55 days after the vote.
forecasts.summary: Israel voted on Oct 27 and no bloc has a majority. The new Knesset sits Nov 10, a candidate gets the mandate by Nov 11, and then has 28 days, extendable to 42. Even the clearest result in recent years took 58 days. This forecast says the waiting is the story, not who wins.
why_now: Mandate assigned by Nov 11, then 28–42 days

base_rate.text: Since 2013, every election that produced a government took 55–82 days to swearing-in, and both 2019 elections produced none. Dec 1 is day 35. Allowing for a surprise unity deal: 95%.

adjustments.label: The president is pushing hard for a fast unity government
The likely first nominee has refused to serve under the current prime minister, making a quick unity deal harder

increase_if: Parties rule out serving with each other
Talk of a second election
decrease_if: A major party breaks from its bloc in the first week
A national-unity framework announced before Nov 11
forecasts.skeptic: Wartime pressure could force an unusually fast unity deal, and the president has said he'd push for one.
forecasts.escalation: Without a majority bloc, this looks more like 2019, when two elections in a row produced no government at all.
forecasts.adjudicator: Even under pressure, the statutory sequence makes a government by Dec 1 nearly impossible. Hold very high.

resolution.condition: As of 11:59 p.m. Israel time on Dec 1, 2026, no new government has won a Knesset confidence vote and been sworn in following the Oct 27, 2026 election, as reported by the Knesset, Reuters, AP or the Times of Israel.
ambiguous: The caretaker government continuing counts as no new government.
A government sworn in on Dec 1 itself resolves no.

forecasts.research_question: Link the 2013, 2015, 2020 and 2021 formation timelines as evidence to firm up the base rate.

history.reason: +1: both camps expect a first nominee who has ruled out serving under the current prime minister.
